title: A line through two points
steps: The direction from \((-3,1)\) to \((1,4)\) is \((4,3)\). Using \((-3,1)\) as a point gives the line equation in option D.

title: Negating an existential statement
steps: Negating “there exists an integer whose square is odd” gives “for every integer, its square is not odd”. An integer square is either odd or even.
answer: B: \(\forall x\in\mathbb Z,\ x^2\text{ is even}.\)

title: Square roots of a complex number
steps: Squaring \(2-i\) gives \(4-4i+i^2=3-4i\). Its negative is the other square root.

title: Amplitude from the speed equation
steps: The speed is zero at the turning points: \(-x^2+2x+8=0\), so \(x=-2\) or \(x=4\). The midpoint is \(1\), and the distance from it to either turning point is \(3\).

title: Writing a contrapositive
steps:
For \(P\Rightarrow Q\), the contrapositive is \(
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P\). Here \(
eg Q\) is \(x>0\), and \(
eg P\) is \(x^2-2x<0\).

title: Moduli of sums and differences
steps: For unit complex numbers, \(|z+w|^2+|z-w|^2=2|z|^2+2|w|^2=4\). Therefore \(|z-w|^2=4-\frac94=\frac74\).

title: Arguments subtended by a circle
steps: The points \(z-2i\) form the circle of radius \(1\) centred at \(-2i\). From the origin, its tangent rays make angles \(\arcsin(1/2)=\pi/6\) on either side of the direction \(-\pi/2\).

title: Acceleration as a function of displacement
steps: Since \(a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}=v\frac{dv}{dx}\), acceleration is zero where the velocity is zero or has a stationary point. The displayed velocity curve has three zeros and two turning points, with acceleration negative at the far left and positive at the far right; graph A has this pattern.

title: Classifying a complex quadrilateral
steps: The relation \(v+z=u+w\) says the diagonals have the same midpoint, so \(UVWZ\) is a parallelogram. Also \(u-w=ki(v-z)\), so its diagonals are perpendicular. A parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus.

title: Reparametrising a space curve
steps: Set the parameter in option D to \(s=2t+\pi/2\). It ranges over all real values, and the coordinates become \((\cos s,s,-\sin s)\), the same helix as \((\cos t,-t,\sin t)\) after taking \(s=-t\).

title: Conjugate and rotated complex numbers
steps: Write \(z=a+ib\), with \(a,b>0\) as shown. Then \(\bar z=a-ib\), the reflection of \(z\) in the real axis, while \(i\bar z=b+ia\), at coordinates \((b,a)\). Mark both points on the diagram.
answer: \(\bar z\) is the reflection of \(z\) across the real axis; \(i\bar z\) is the point \((b,a)\), in the first quadrant.

title: Multiplying complex numbers in polar form
steps: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments: \(wz=(2\cdot3)e^{i(\pi/6+\pi/6)}=6e^{i\pi/3}\).

title: Squaring a complex number
steps: Expand \((x+iy)^2\) and use \(i^2=-1\).

title: Taking a complex reciprocal
steps: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(x-iy\) to make the denominator real.

title: Resolving a force along a vector
steps: The direction vector has magnitude \(\sqrt{2^2+(-2)^2+1^2}=3\). Scale it by \(12/3=4\) to obtain the force vector.

title: Dot product of force and displacement
steps: Take the componentwise dot product with \(\mathbf d=(1,1,2)\): \(2+4+8\cdot2=22\).

title: Proof by contradiction with surds
steps: Assume the negation, \(\sqrt3+\sqrt5\leq\sqrt{11}\). Squaring positive sides gives \(8+2\sqrt{15}\leq11\), hence \(2\sqrt{15}\leq3\). Squaring again gives \(60\leq9\), a contradiction.

title: Completing the square in an integral
steps: Complete the square: \(7-x^2-6x=16-(x+3)^2\). Apply the standard inverse-sine integral with the substitution \(u=(x+3)/4\).

title: A definite integral by parts
steps: Choose \(u=x\) and \(dv=\sin x\,dx\), so \(du=dx\) and \(v=-\cos x\). Integration by parts gives \(\int_0^{\pi/2}x\sin x\,dx=[-x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}+\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx\).
The product term is zero at both endpoints. The remaining integral is \([\sin x]_0^{\pi/2}=1\).

title: Induction for higher derivatives
steps: For \(n=1\), the product rule gives \(y^{\prime}=(2x+1)e^{2x}\), agreeing with the proposed expression.
Assume \(y^{(k)}=(2^kx+k2^{k-1})e^{2x}\) for some integer \(k\ge1\). Differentiating gives \(y^{(k+1)}=[2^k+2(2^kx+k2^{k-1})]e^{2x}\).
Simplifying yields \([2^{k+1}x+(k+1)2^k]e^{2x}\), exactly the statement for \(k+1\). Therefore induction proves the formula for every positive integer.

title: A half-plane from complex distances
steps: Write \(z=x+iy\). Squaring both non-negative distances gives \((x+5)^2+(y-1)^2>(x-3)^2+(y+3)^2\).

After cancellation, \(16x-8y+8>0\), or \(y<2x+1\). Sketch the line through \((-1/2,0)\) and \((0,1)\) as a dashed boundary, then shade the side below it. The origin is a useful test point in the shaded half-plane.
answer: The open half-plane \(y<2x+1\); its boundary is excluded.

title: Partial fractions with a quadratic factor
steps: Write the fraction as \(A/(4-x)+(Bx+C)/(x^2+1)\). Multiplication by the denominator gives \(x^2-2x+9=A(x^2+1)+(Bx+C)(4-x)\).
Substituting \(x=4\) gives \(A=1\). Setting \(x=0\) then gives \(C=2\); comparing the squared terms gives \(B=0\). Thus the integrand is \(1/(4-x)+2/(x^2+1)\).
Integrate each term, allowing for the negative derivative of \(4-x\).

title: Stopping distance under resistance
steps: Take distance \(s\) along the initial direction of travel. Before the particle stops, Newton’s law and \(a=v\,dv/ds\) give \(v\,dv/ds=-(k+v^2)\), after cancelling the mass.
Separate variables and integrate from initial speed \(V_0\) to zero: \(S=-\int_{V_0}^{0}v/(k+v^2)\,dv=-\tfrac12[\ln(k+v^2)]_{V_0}^{0}\).
The logarithms combine into a ratio. Since \(k>0\), the result is non-negative.

title: Reflecting the limits of an integral
steps: Use \(u=m-x\), so \(dx=-du\). The lower endpoint \(x=m-4\) becomes \(u=4\), and the upper endpoint \(x=m-2\) becomes \(u=2\).
Also \(e^{-x}=e^{-m}e^u\) and \(x-m+1=1-u\). Consequently the transformed integral is \(e^{-m}\int_4^2 e^u/(u-1)\,du\).
Reversing the endpoints introduces a minus sign, leaving the integral defining \(A\).

title: A unit vector perpendicular to two vectors
steps: Perpendicularity gives \(2x+4y-3z=0\) and \(-4x-5y+3z=0\). Adding them gives \(y=-2x\); substituting into the first equation gives \(z=-2x\).
The unit-length condition is \(x^2+y^2+z^2=1\). Hence \(9x^2=1\), so \(x=\pm1/3\), with \(y\) and \(z\) carrying the opposite signs.

title: Proving the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality
steps: Since \(a,b>0\), the square \((\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\) is non-negative. Expanding gives \(a+b-2\sqrt{ab}\ge0\). Divide by 2.
Equality holds exactly when \(a=b\).

title: A strict inequality from distinct inputs
steps: Apply part (i) to \(a=2n+1\) and \(b=2n+3\). Both are positive for \(n\ge0\), and they differ, so \(\sqrt{(2n+1)(2n+3)}<2n+2\).
Divide by the positive quantity \((2n+2)\sqrt{2n+3}\), then multiply by \(\sqrt{2n+1}\), to obtain the required comparison.

title: Symmetry followed by a half-angle substitution
steps: Call the given integral \(J\). First substitute \(u=\pi/2-x\). Since sine and cosine exchange, \(J=\int_0^{\pi/2}(\pi/2-x)/(1+\sin x+\cos x)\,dx\).
Adding this expression to the original gives \(2J=(\pi/2)K\), where \(K=\int_0^{\pi/2}dx/(1+\sin x+\cos x)\). Thus \(J=\pi K/4\).
For \(K\), put \(t=\tan(x/2)\). The endpoints become 0 and 1, and the half-angle identities reduce the integrand to \(dt/(1+t)\). Hence \(K=[\ln(1+t)]_0^1=\ln2\).

title: Reducing an integral of an even cotangent power
steps: Separate the final factor of \(\cot^2\theta\), and replace it by \(\csc^2\theta-1\):
\[I_n=\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\cot^{2n-2}\theta\,\csc^2\theta\,d\theta-I_{n-1}.\]
The substitution \(u=\cot\theta\) integrates the first term as \(-\cot^{2n-1}\theta/(2n-1)\). Its upper value is zero and its lower value is \(-1/(2n-1)\).

title: Applying a reduction formula twice
steps: The starting integral is \(I_0=\pi/4\). Thus \(I_1=1-\pi/4\), and \(I_2=1/3-I_1\).

title: Velocity from acceleration as a function of position
steps: Use \(a=v\,dv/dx\): \(v\,dv=32x(x^2+3)\,dx\). Integration gives \(v^2=16(x^2+3)^2+C\).
The initial conditions \(x=0\), \(v=-12\) give \(C=0\). The velocity starts negative and its magnitude never vanishes, so retain the negative branch throughout.

title: Travel time with position-dependent velocity
steps: The velocity is always negative, so travelling 3 metres from the origin means reaching \(x=-3\). Since \(dt=dx/v\),
\[t=-\frac14\int_0^{-3}\frac{dx}{x^2+3}=-\frac1{4\sqrt3}\left[\tan^{-1}(x/\sqrt3)\right]_0^{-3}.\]
The inverse tangent at the lower displacement is \(-\pi/3\).

title: Identifying a root of unity
steps: Multiplying the given sum by \(w-1\) makes all intermediate powers cancel, leaving \(w^7-1=0\). Also \(w\ne1\), because substituting 1 into the original sum gives 7.
answer: \(w^7=1\), so \(w\) is a non-trivial seventh root of unity.

title: Conjugate roots written as powers
steps: A non-real root of a polynomial with real coefficients comes with its complex conjugate. Hence the second root is \(\overline{w+w^2+w^4}\).
Every root of unity has modulus 1, so \(\overline w=1/w=w^6\). Reduce exponents modulo 7: \(\overline w^{\,2}=w^{12}=w^5\) and \(\overline w^{\,4}=w^{24}=w^3\).

title: The product of conjugate roots
steps: The constant term is the product of the roots. Expanding \((w+w^2+w^4)(w^3+w^5+w^6)\) and using \(w^7=1\) gives \(3+w+w^2+\cdots+w^6\). The original relation says the six non-constant powers sum to \(-1\).

title: Comparing sums of reciprocal arithmetic terms
steps: Let \(u=1/a>0\). The four reciprocal terms are \(u,u+k,u+2k,u+3k\), so
\[a+d-b-c=\left(\frac1u-\frac1{u+k}\right)-\left(\frac1{u+2k}-\frac1{u+3k}\right).\]
This is \(\dfrac{k}{u(u+k)}-\dfrac{k}{(u+2k)(u+3k)}\). The second denominator is strictly larger than the first because \(u,k>0\). The difference is therefore positive.

title: Area of a parallelogram using a scalar product
steps: The side lengths satisfy \(|\mathbf a|^2=4^2+3^2+(-1)^2=26\) and \(|\mathbf b|^2=2^2+(-1)^2+3^2=14\). Their scalar product is \(8-3-3=2\).
If \(\phi\) is the angle between them, \(\cos\phi=2/\sqrt{26\cdot14}\). Hence
\[\text{Area}^2=|\mathbf a|^2|\mathbf b|^2\sin^2\phi=26\cdot14-2^2=360.\]
Take the positive square root for an area.

title: Maximum acceleration in simple harmonic motion
steps: Two cycles per second means frequency \(f=2\), so the angular frequency is \(\omega=2\pi f=4\pi\).
For SHM, \(v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)\) and \(v_{\max}=\omega A\). At \(|x|=1/4\), the given half-speed condition gives \(\omega^2A^2/4=\omega^2(A^2-1/16)\).
Therefore \(3A^2/4=1/16\), so \(A=1/(2\sqrt3)\). The acceleration is \(-\omega^2x\), whose largest positive value occurs at \(x=-A\).

title: A complex ratio and the half-angle formula
steps: Write \(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta=e^{i\theta}\). Factoring out \(e^{i\theta/2}\) from numerator and denominator gives
\[\frac{1+e^{i\theta}}{1-e^{i\theta}}=\frac{e^{-i\theta/2}+e^{i\theta/2}}{e^{-i\theta/2}-e^{i\theta/2}}=\frac{2\cos(\theta/2)}{-2i\sin(\theta/2)}.\]
Since \(1/(-i)=i\), the result is \(i\cot(\theta/2)\). Both expressions require \(\theta\notin2\pi\mathbb Z\).

title: Sixth roots by De Moivre’s theorem
steps: If \(w^6=-1\), then \(|w|^6=1\), so \(|w|=1\). Write \(w=\cos\phi+i\sin\phi\).
De Moivre’s theorem gives \(w^6=\cos6\phi+i\sin6\phi\). To equal \(-1\), the angle must satisfy \(6\phi=(2j+1)\pi\). The six values \(j=0,\ldots,5\) give all distinct roots.

title: Mapping the six roots to the required solutions
steps: Put \(w=(z-1)/(z+1)\). Then \(w^6=-1\), so use one of the six roots in part (ii). Rearranging gives \(z=(1+w)/(1-w)\). No sixth root of \(-1\) equals 1, so this denominator is non-zero.
Apply part (i) with \(\theta=(2j+1)\pi/6\). The half-angle is \((2j+1)\pi/12\), producing six distinct values.

title: Bounding complex roots with the triangle inequality
steps: Suppose, for a contradiction, that a solution has \(|z|\le1/2\). Write the left side as \(\sum_{j=1}^{n}z^j\cos(j\theta)\).
The triangle inequality and \(|\cos(j\theta)|\le1\) imply
\[1=\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}z^j\cos(j\theta)\right|\le\sum_{j=1}^{n}|z|^j\le\sum_{j=1}^{n}2^{-j}=1-2^{-n}<1.\]
This is impossible. The finite geometric sum is strictly less than 1, so the contradiction excludes the boundary as well as the interior.

title: Projectile motion with linear resistance
steps: The launch components are \(\dot x(0)=50(4/5)=40\) and \(\dot y(0)=-50(3/5)=-30\). Solving \(\ddot x=-k\dot x\) and using \(x(0)=0\) gives
\[\dot x=40e^{-kt},\qquad x=\frac{40}{k}(1-e^{-kt}).\]
For the vertical component, \(\dot y+10/k\) decays exponentially. The initial velocity and \(y(0)=0\) therefore give
Eliminate time using \(e^{-kt}=1-kx/40\) and \(t=-\ln(1-kx/40)/k\).

title: The closest point on a line
steps: Minimising distance is equivalent to minimising its square. Since \(|\mathbf d|=1\),
\[f(\lambda)^2=|\mathbf a-\mathbf b+\lambda\mathbf d|^2=|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|^2+2\lambda(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\cdot\mathbf d+\lambda^2.\]
This quadratic opens upwards. Its derivative vanishes at \(2(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\cdot\mathbf d+2\lambda=0\), giving the unique minimum.

title: The shortest connecting segment is perpendicular
steps: The connecting vector is \(\overrightarrow{PB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a-\lambda_0\mathbf d\). Its scalar product with \(\mathbf d\) is \((\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf d-\lambda_0|\mathbf d|^2=\lambda_0-\lambda_0=0\).
answer: \(\overrightarrow{PB}\cdot\mathbf d=0\), so PB is perpendicular to the line direction.

title: Distance between a line and a sphere
steps: First find the line’s distance from the origin. Using part (i) with \(\mathbf b=\mathbf0\), the closest point has vector \(\mathbf p_0=\mathbf a-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf d)\mathbf d\).
Because \(|\mathbf d|=1\), its distance from the origin is \(D=\sqrt{|\mathbf a|^2-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf d)^2}\).

If \(D>1\), move one unit from the origin towards this closest point to reach the sphere; the remaining gap is \(D-1\). If \(D\le1\), the line intersects or touches the sphere, so the shortest distance is zero.
